title: Predict next year's build time

blocks.text: A regional utility (fictional, like GridCap) times its model builder on four portfolio sizes this year and wants to know two things before next year's merger quadruples the portfolio: how fast the build time grows, and roughly how long the merged portfolio will take to build.

If the build takes about $`t = c\, n^{a}`$ seconds for $`n`$ projects, then $`\log t = a \log n + \log c`$: a straight line in $`(\log n, \log t)`$ whose slope is the growth exponent $`a`$ and whose intercept is $`\log c`$. Real measurements are noisy, so no line passes through all of them; take the least-squares line, the one that makes the sum of squared vertical distances smallest. For points $`(x_j, y_j)`$ with means $`\bar x`$ and $`\bar y`$ its slope and intercept are
a = \frac{\sum_j (x_j - \bar x)(y_j - \bar y)}{\sum_j (x_j - \bar x)^2}, \qquad \log c = \bar y - a\, \bar x

items: `fit(sizes, seconds)` returns `(a, c)`, fitted as above on $`x_j = \log n_j`$ and $`y_j = \log t_j`$ (natural logarithms, `math.log`);
`predict(sizes, seconds, n)` returns the fitted curve's time for `n` projects, $`c\, n^a`$.

blocks.text: The measurements may come in any order. The tests use made-up times, so no clock is involved. Run the file to see a prediction. About eight lines.

from __future__ import annotations

import math


def fit(sizes: list[int], seconds: list[float]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """(a, c) with seconds ≈ c * size ** a, fitted by least squares on log(seconds) against log(size)."""
    xs = [math.log(n) for n in sizes]
    ys = [math.log(t) for t in seconds]
    mx, my = sum(xs) / len(xs), sum(ys) / len(ys)
    a = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in xs)
    c = math.exp(my - a * mx)
    return a, c


def predict(sizes: list[int], seconds: list[float], n: int) -> float:
    """The time the fitted curve gives for a portfolio of n projects."""
    a, c = fit(sizes, seconds)
    return c * n ** a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sizes, seconds = [1_000, 2_000, 4_000, 8_000], [0.31, 1.05, 4.2, 16.9]
    a, c = fit(sizes, seconds)
    print(f"exponent {a:.2f}; 40,000 projects would take about {predict(sizes, seconds, 40_000):,.0f} s")

cases.says: times that follow c times n to the power a exactly give back a and c, and the prediction at a new size
the exponent is the least-squares slope over every measurement, not the slope between the smallest and the largest
measurements given in any order give the same exponent and constant
the prediction comes from the fitted curve, not from scaling the last measurement

concepts: the slope of log time against log size, fitted over several sizes, says how a build grows
